A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work on predicting LM behavior using input-state probes and conformal calibration. The main texts, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–C are readable, as is v2's additional checklist.

before.justification: V1 reports original behavior-prediction and CoT acceleration experiments, parameter ablations, and evaluations on multiple model families.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical evaluations and reports additional BERT comparisons and a revised safety intervention experiment.

M1.justification: The linear input-state probe and calibration rule remain unchanged. The safety application changes procedurally: v1 predicts whether the LM will abstain, while v2 trains on responding instances to predict whether it should have abstained and forces abstention for predicted failures (Section 4.1 and Appendix C.2.2).

E1.justification: The dataset roster is retained, but the task on SelfAware, KnownUnknown, and WildJailbreak changes substantially. V1 predicts the LM's refusal decision; v2 evaluates inappropriate answering/compliance using answerability or maliciousness labels and tests a forced-abstention intervention. This changes the prediction requirements of the safety evaluation.

E2.justification: V2 adds a fine-tuned bert-large-uncased input-text classifier to formatting, confidence-estimation, and safety comparisons (Figures 2–3 and Table 1). V1 has no corresponding trained text-only comparator. Vanilla CoT remains the acceleration comparator; speculative decoding is discussed but not evaluated as a baseline.

E3.justification: The revised safety evaluation conditions on answered/complied-with instances and adds precision, recall, and residual jailbreak-success measurements, replacing the earlier refusal-prediction evaluation. V2 also reports alpha=0.8 alongside alpha=0.9 for formatting and confidence estimation. These changes prevent treating the safety scores as directly comparable performance gains.

E4.justification: Most training-size, layer, threshold, model-size, and cross-model analyses are retained or relocated to Appendices A–B. V2 removes the confidence-versus-token-position curve, the input-length correlation result, and the HealthVER layer-ablation panel. It adds threshold comparisons for formatting and confidence-estimation tasks.

E5.justification: V1 shows whiskers and shaded bands without specifying seeds or their statistical meaning. V2 Figure 2 and checklist item 7 explicitly report five seeds, variation from training/validation splits, mean aggregation, and 2σ intervals/significance claims. This substantially expands uncertainty documentation; it does not establish an increase in runs.

E6.justification: V2 adds BERT and alpha=0.8 results and replaces the main abstention-prediction results with safety-failure results, including a reported WildJailbreak success reduction from 30% to 2.7%. Confidence-estimation values also change: MSMarco verbalized-confidence coverage is 31.13% in v1 Figure 4e versus 42% in v2 Figure 3 at alpha=0.9. The headline 65% CoT cost reduction, 1.34% worst accuracy loss, and Appendix A Mistral/DeepSeek scores are retained.

T1.justification: Sections 2 and 3.1 retain the same score function, quantile construction, exchangeability assumption, probability bound, and calibration inequality in Equations 1–3. No original theorem or proof is added; v2's checklist explicitly identifies the theoretical results as borrowed.

C1.justification: V2 makes preventing safety-alignment failures a central contribution and adds the headline claim of reducing jailbreaking by 91%, beyond v1's emphasis on predicting behavior and accelerating CoT. The introduction also strengthens the data-efficiency claim from fewer than 1,000 to fewer than 500 training instances. The central predictive-capability and CoT acceleration claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds a substantive argument that probe-based acceleration can complement speculative decoding and architectural optimizations (Section 5), and interprets the revised safety task as an intervention against disproportionately costly errors. It drops the early-token miscalibration interpretation while retaining the limitations concerning longer outputs and knowledge unavailable to the LM.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents balanced formatting train/test samples, deterministic greedy decoding, approximately two hours to generate hidden states for 10,000 instances, and probe training under 30 seconds. Appendix C clarifies GPU memory, while the checklist adds code-access and hidden-state-data availability information. These disclosures do not establish changes to previously unspecified settings.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around guardrails, alignment, introspection, response planning, and conformal prediction applications. Section 7 discusses works such as Looking Inward, Emergent Response Planning, and Future Lens, refining v1's broad priority claim toward the combination of hidden-state probes and conformal early-warning systems.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around early warning and safety. Section 3 replaces the MCQA running example with formatting failures, safety applications precede CoT acceleration, and Section 6 consolidates the ablation narrative. Appendix B gains subsections, and acknowledgments and a conference checklist are added.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn around safety intervention. V1's stacked early-warning plots are replaced by grouped comparison bars and a safety table; separate IID/OOD acceleration panels are merged. Ablation panels are reorganized between the main text and Appendix B, while the standalone MCQA consistency figure and selected diagnostic panels disappear.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical assessability by adding trained input-text controls where v1 lacked them, explaining five-seed uncertainty reporting, and evaluating a concrete safety intervention. Clearer research positioning and implementation disclosures further improve the paper. These gains outweigh the removal of several diagnostics. Some overstatement remains: Table 1 gives KnownUnknown recall of 72.8% for the probe versus 93.1% for BERT, contrary to the blanket outperformance claim, and the revised safety results concern a filtered task.
